title: KV cache resize & throttling regression - post-incident notes
summary: On 2025-11-05 we saw a multi-hour degradation impacting serving pools running continuous batching for <model-redwood/ggml-v2>. Symptoms included repeated OOM kills, rising tail latency, and degraded throughput. The proximate trigger was a KV cache resize operation that coincided with a continuous-batching path regression; together these produced sustained memory growth and compaction work that pushed pods over node memory limits. This document captures timeline, mitigation steps, analysis, a draft runbook for similar events, and proposed action items.
timeline:
2025-11-05T02:47Z - Alert: node-memory-high (pools: batch-us-west-2-pool-7)
2025-11-05T02:49Z - First pod OOM (serving-runtime:worker) and restart seen in cluster metrics
2025-11-05T02:51Z - Latency SLO breaches spike for routes using model ggml-v2 (p95 from 120ms -> 520ms)
2025-11-05T02:55Z - Pager dispatched to eng-sre oncall (Nakul)
2025-11-05T03:03Z - Initial mitigation: reduced max_batch_size via runtime feature-flag on affected pool (rollout id ff-2025-11-05-1)
2025-11-05T03:18Z - OOMs continue; memory growth not reversing. Observed frequent cache_resizer jobs starting and overlapping
2025-11-05T03:35Z - Disabled background compaction for kv-cache (hotfix ff-2025-11-05-2) which immediately slowed memory growth
2025-11-05T04:10Z - Autoscaler paused for the pool; traffic gradually shifted to fallback nodes and latency recovered to baseline by 04:40Z
2025-11-05T05:40Z - Incident declared mitigated; follow-up investigation started
symptoms:
- Repeated worker OOM kills across 6 pods in the pool
- Gradual but persistent RSS increase over 30-90 minutes prior to first OOM
- Alerts: node-memory-high, pod-restarts-high, route-latency-slo-exceeded
- Logs: frequent 'kv_cache:resize started' entries interleaved with 'compaction:begin' and then sharp memory jumps
- Heap/profile snapshots show large live allocation in kv-index structures and compaction buffers
detection_and_alerting: Current alerts fired correctly (node-memory-high, pod-restarts-high). Gaps: there is no alert specifically for 'concurrent-kv-resize-job-count' or for 'kv-cache-growth-rate' which would have captured the early slope. Also no alert for compaction-duration > threshold. Detection improvement candidates are listed in action items below.
initial_mitigation:
- Reduced max_batch_size for the affected pool via feature flag to prevent large per-request cache growth
- Disabled kv-cache background compaction process (hotfix) to stop work that amplified RSS spikes
- Paused autoscaler to avoid creating new pods that would immediately get OOMed
- Routed a percentage of traffic to an older model variant (ggml-v2-slim) to reduce cache pressure
Notes: the compaction disable was a high-confidence, targeted change. It had the expected effect of flattening memory growth within ~10 minutes and stopped new OOMs.
root_cause: Primary: Race between KV cache resize and background compaction combined with a continuous-batching regression that increased effective per-request key volume. Resize path was implemented to be optimistic and could spawn overlapping resize jobs without global coordination. Compaction assumed a stable index shape; overlapping resize+compaction could allocate transient buffers proportional to index deltas, producing memory amplification. Secondary: continuous-batching change increased average prefix lengths (more cached keys per request), which pushed indices into resize paths more frequently. Tertiary: alerts/telemetry lacked signals for resize concurrency and compaction latencies.
postmortem_analysis:
- Heap diffs: dominant growth in kv_index::buckets and compaction temp buffers.
- Recreated locally by running high-concurrency continuous-batching harness with synthetic workload; reproduced when resize >= 2 concurrent jobs allowed.
- Memory profile shows transient allocations up to 1.8x steady-state during compaction+resize overlap.
- Code review: resize uses an atomic 'in_progress' bit per-shard but doesn't back off if another job is already allocating; multiple shards can be resized concurrently leading to peak transient usage.
- CI/bench gap: no test covered long-running compaction under high-concurrency continuous-batch workloads; this workload shape wasn't in perf benchmarks.
runbook_draft:
(Quick triage)
1) Alert fires: check pods in pool (kubectl get pods -n serving -l pool=<pool>). If >2 pods OOMing in 10m, proceed.
2) Identify recent feature flags: check flag rollout for 'batching' and 'kv-cache' ops (ff dashboard).
3) Mitigate: first reduce max_batch_size via ff to 50% of current value across pool.
4) If OOMs continue: disable kv-cache compaction via runtime flag and set 'kv.compaction.enabled=false' for the pool.
5) Pause autoscaler for pool: runtime-admin pause-autoscaler <pool>.
6) Route 15-30% of traffic to fallback model variant (configured in routing policies) to relieve cache pressure.
7) If memory growth persists, evacuate node by cordoning and draining (kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets).
8) Collect artifacts before restart: pmap, /proc/<pid>/smaps, runtime heap profile dump command (runtime-admin heap-dump <pid>), and core if available. Upload to incident folder.
(Recovery verification)
- Monitor heap slope for 20m. If flattening and SLOs returning, keep compaction disabled and schedule controlled re-enable after a fix.
(Post-incident)
- Add 'kv-cache-resize-concurrency' and 'compaction-duration' alerts.
- Create playback to test re-enable path in staging with synthetic load.

notes_to_self:
- Why did the resize jobs not log an error when they overlapped? Add better logging around 'resize reason' and concurrent job id.
- Investigate whether certain model prompt shapes are disproportionately causing index growth; ask solutions-eng to share customer workloads that were active during the incident.
- Evaluate if a memory cap for compaction temp buffers is possible.
- Follow up: confirm whether the autoscaler created new pods that inherited flags incorrectly (ff scoping) - seen previously in ENG-SRV-134.
- Slack thread: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C0123456/p1634123456789000 has raw oncall messages and command outputs.
